title: Definition
body_md:
We say that a group $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$, for some $k \geq 1$, if
for every $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_k \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$, there exists a bijection  $f$ of $G$ such that every map $g \mapsto \beta_i(g)f(g)$  is a bijection  of $G$.
head: environment

label: Thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:main}
Assume $G$ is a finite group. Let $p$ be the smallest prime divisor of the order $|G|$ of $G$. Then $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$ for all $1 \leq k <p-1$.
head: environment

label: col:commonTrans+Mate
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{col:commonTrans+Mate}
     Let $G$ be a finite group whose smallest prime divisor is $p$. If $k < p -1$, then for any automorphisms $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_k \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$  the Latin squares $L_i(x,y)=\beta_i(x)y$ have a common transversal and a common orthogonal mate.
head: environment

label: prop: Extension-property
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: Extension-property}
    Assume $N $ is a characteristic subgroup of the finite group $G$. If $N$ and $G/N$ satisfy property $\mathcal{P}_k$ for some integer $k$ then $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We clearly can assume that $N < G$. Let $\{\beta_i\}_{i \leq k}$ be automorphisms of $G$. 
 Since $N$ is characteristic in $G$ and each $\beta_i \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$, each $\beta_i$ induces an automorphism $\bar{\beta}_i \in \mathrm{Aut}(G/N)$ defined by 
\[
\bar{\beta}_i(gN) := \beta_i(g) N.
\]

Because $G/N$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$,  there exists a bijection $\bar{\theta} : G/N \to G/N$ such that 
\[
gN \to \bar{\beta}_i(gN)\bar{\theta}(gN) 
\]
 is a bijection of $G/N$ for all $i=1, \dots , k$.



Let $T$ be a transversal of $N$ in $G$. Since $\bar{\theta}$ is a bijection of $G/N$, there exists a permutation $\sigma$ of $T$  such that 
\[
\bar{\theta}(t N) = \sigma(t) N,
\]
for all $t \in T$. We also note  that  every element $g \in G$ is written uniquely as $g= tn$ with  $t \in T$ and $n \in N$.

Now fix $t \in T$ and observe that for every $i =1, \dots, k$, the map $\alpha_{i,t}: G \to G$ defined as 
\[
\alpha_{i,t}(g)= \sigma(t)^{-1} \beta_i(g) \sigma(t),
\]
is also an automorphism of $G$ because $\beta_i$ is. Furthermore,  
each restriction $ \alpha_{i,t} |_N $ lies in $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$, because  $N$ is characteristic subgroup in $G$. Now $N$ also satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$ hence  we obtain  a bijection  $\phi_t $  such  that, for each $i=1, \dots, k$,  the map
\[
N \ni n \to \alpha_{i,t}(n)\phi_t(n)
\]
is a bijection  of $N$.

We define $f: G \to G$ as 
\[
f(tn):= \sigma(t) \phi_t(n)
\]
for every $t \in T$ and $n \in N$ and we claim that $f$ is a bijection of $G$. Indeed, assume 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f-bijection}
\sigma(t) \phi_t(n)= \sigma(t') \phi_{t'}(n')
\end{equation}
where $(t, n) \neq (t',n')$. Since $T$ is a transversal of $N$ and $\phi_t ( n), \phi_{t'}(n') \in N$, we must have $\sigma(t) = \sigma(t')$, which implies $t=t'$. Equation   \eqref{eq:f-bijection} then simplifies to $\phi_t(n)= \phi_{t}(n')$. As $\phi_t$ is a bijection, it follows that $n=n'$, contradicting our initial assumption and thus proving our  claim.

To complete the proof, it remains to show that $\beta_i(tn) f(tn)$ is a bijection of $G$,  for every $i=1, \dots, k$. Assume $g\neq g'$ are  distinct elements of $G$, with $g =tn$  and $g'=t'n'$, so  $(t,n) \neq (t',n')$. If 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:b_if-bijection}
    \beta_i(tn)\sigma(t)\phi_t(n)= \beta_i(t'n')\sigma(t')\phi_{t'}(n') 
\end{equation}
then      $\bar{\beta}_i(tN) \bar{\theta}(tN)= \bar{\beta}_i(t'N) \bar{\theta}(t'N)$. 
Hence $tN= t'N$ as $gN \to \bar{\beta}_i(gN)\bar{\theta}(gN) $
 is a bijection of $G/N$ and so $t=t'$, as $T$ is a transversal.  Thus  \eqref{eq:b_if-bijection} implies that 
\[
\sigma(t)^{-1}\beta_{i}(n)\sigma (t) \phi_t(n)= \sigma(t)^{-1}\beta_i(n') \sigma(t) \phi_t(n'),
\] 
since $\beta_i$ is an automorphism of $G$.  So   $ \alpha_{i,t}(n)\phi_t(n)= \alpha_{i,t}(n')\phi_t(n')$ and thus $n=n'$, as the map $n \to \alpha_{i,t}(n)\phi_t(n)$ is a bijection. This leads to $(t,n)= (t',n')$, a contradiction that completes the proof of the proposition.
head: environment

label: Thm:AutAbelian
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:AutAbelian}
    Let  $G \cong \mathbf{Z}_{p^{e_1}} \times \cdots \times \mathbf{Z}_{p^{e_n}}$ be an abelian $p$-group, with $1 \leq e_1 \leq  \cdots \leq e_n$. Then the map $\psi: R_G \to \mathrm{End}(G)$  defined as  
    \[
\psi(A) (\overline{h}_1,\dots,\overline{h}_n)^T= \pi\big(A(h_1, \cdots, h_n)^T\big)
    \]
    is a surjective ring  homomorphism. Furthermore an endomorphism $\beta= \psi(A)$ of $G$ is an automorphism if and only if the reduction of  $ A$ modulo $p $  is invertible in $GL_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$.
head: environment

label: Thm:k<p-1-abelian-p-case
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:k<p-1-abelian-p-case}
  Assume $G$ is a finite abelian $p$-group and $k < p-1$ an integer. If $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_k$ are automorphisms of $G$, then there exists an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for each $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, the map $g \mapsto \beta_i(g)+f(g)$ is an automorphism of $G$. Consequently, $G$ satisfies property $\mathcal{P}_k$ for all $k < p-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First assume that $G \cong \mathbb Z_{p^e}^n$ is a homocyclic $p$-group. By \autoref{Thm:AutAbelian}, for each automorphism $\beta_i$ there exists a matrix $A_i \in R_G$, where $R_G=\mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{Z})$ in the homocyclic case, such that $\beta_i=\psi(A_i)$ and $A_i \bmod p$ is non-singular, for all $i=1,\dots,k$. We observe that it is enough to find a matrix $B\in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{Z}))$ such that both $B\bmod p$ and $(A_i +B )\bmod p$ are invertible for every $i$, as then $f:=\psi(B)$ will be the required automorphism of $G$.

Define
\begin{equation*}
T=\{X\in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)\mid \det X=0\},
\tag{1}
\end{equation*}
and denote by $\overline{ A_i}$ the reduction of $A_i$ modulo $p$. The condition that $A_i+B$ is invertible modulo $p$ is equivalent to requiring that
\begin{equation*}
\overline{ B} \notin T-\overline{ A_i}
\end{equation*}
for each $i=1,\dots,k$. (By $T-\overline{ A_i}$ we denote the set  consisting of the matrices $ X-\overline{ A_i }$ with  $X \in T $.) 

It is enough to prove that
\begin{equation*}
\big|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)\big| - \big| \bigcup_{i=1}^k (T-\overline{A_i}) \big|>0 .
\end{equation*}

We have
\[
|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)|= 
p^{n^2}\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t}),
\]
and, for each $i$,
\[
|T-\overline {A_i}|=|T|= p^{n^2}-|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|.
\]
Hence
\[
\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^k (T-\overline {A_i})\right|
\leq
k p^{n^2}\left[1-\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t})\right].
\]
Thus
\begin{align}\label{eq:countAutom}
\left|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \right| - \left| \bigcup_{i=1}^k (T-\overline A_i)\right|  &\geq 
p^{n^2}  \left[  \prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t}) -  k\left(1-\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t})\right)  \right] \\
&=  p^{n^2}  \left[ (k+1)\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t})-k \right].
                      
\end{align}


Furthermore,
\begin{align*}
\prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t})
&\geq 1-\sum_{t=1}^n \frac{1}{p^t}  \\
&= 1-\frac{p^{-1}(1-p^{-n})}{1-p^{-1}} \\
&= 1-\frac{1-p^{-n}}{p-1} \\
&=\frac{p-2+p^{-n}}{p-1} > \frac{p-2}{p-1}.
\end{align*}
Since $k\leq p-2$, and the function $x\mapsto x/(x+1)$  is increasing, it follows that
$\frac{p-2}{p-1}\geq \frac{k}{k+1}$. Therefore
$ \prod_{t=1}^n(1-p^{-t})>\frac{k}{k+1}$. Together with \eqref{eq:countAutom}, this gives
\[
\left|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)\right| - \left| \bigcup_{i=1}^k (T-\overline{A_i})\right|>0.
\]
Hence the theorem holds in this homocyclic case.


Now suppose that
 \[
  G \cong (\mathbf{Z}_{p^{e_1}})^{m_1}  \times \cdots \times (\mathbf{Z}_{p^{e_r}})^{m_r}
  \]
where  $1 \leq e_1 < \cdots < e_r$ and $n=m_1+\dots+m_r$.

As earlier, for each automorphism $\beta_i \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ there exists a matrix $A_i \in \mathbf{R}_G$ such that $\beta_i = \psi(A_i)$ and $A_i \bmod p$ is nonsingular,  for all $i=1, \dots, k$. Notice that,  in view of the definition of $R_G$ the reduced matrices  $\overline{A_i}$ are block upper triangular matrices of the form
\[
\overline A_i=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline A_i^{1} & * & \cdots & * \\
0 & \overline A_i^{2} & \cdots & * \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \overline{A}_i^{r}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
where $\overline {A}_i^j \in \mathrm{GL}_{m_j}(\mathbf{F}_p)$, for all $j=1, \dots, r$.

For every fixed $j$, the  argument for the homocyclic case provides an invertible matrix $\overline {B}^j \in \mathrm{GL}_{m_j}(\mathbf{F}_p)$ such that the matrices  $\overline{A}_i^j + \overline{B}^j  $ are all invertible and thus elements in $\mathrm{GL}_{m_j}(\mathbf{F}_p)$.

Now define the block diagonal matrix
\[
\overline B:=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline B^{1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \overline B^{2} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \overline B^{r}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Clearly $ \overline B\in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$, because all its diagonal blocks are invertible.

Moreover, for every $i=1,\dots,k$, the matrix $\overline A_i + \overline B $ is again block upper triangular, and its diagonal blocks are precisely $\overline A_i^{j} + \overline B^{j} $,  for  $ j=1,\dots,r$.
These blocks are invertible by construction. Hence
\[
\overline A_i + \overline B\,  \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)  \, \, 
\text{for all } i=1,\dots,k.
\]

Choose a matrix $B\in R_G$ whose reduction modulo $p$ is $\overline B$. This is possible since $\overline B$ is block diagonal, so it is compatible with the divisibility conditions defining $R_G$. By \autoref{Thm:AutAbelian}, the map $f:=\psi(B) $ is an automorphism of $G$. 
Furthermore, for every $i=1,\dots,k$, the reduction of $A_i + B $ modulo $p$ is
$\overline A_i + \overline B$  which is non-singular.  Therefore, again by \autoref{Thm:AutAbelian}, the map 
$\beta_i +f =\psi(A_i + B )$  is an automorphism of $G$, for every $i=1,\dots,k$.

Hence $f$ has the desired properties, and the proof of the theorem is complete.
head: environment

label: Prop.Homocyclic.k=p-1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop.Homocyclic.k=p-1}
    Assume $G$ is a noncyclic homocyclic  $p$-group. If $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_{p-1}$ are automorphisms of $G$, then there exists an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for each $i \in \{1, \dots, {p-1}\}$, the map $g \mapsto \beta_i(g)+f(g)$ is an automorphism  of $G$. Consequently, $G$ satisfies property $\mathcal{P}_{p-1}$.
head: environment

label: eq.sum-invertible-eigenvalue1
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G = \mathbf{Z}_{p^e}^n$ for $n \geq 2$. Following the notation from the proof of Theorem \ref{Thm:k<p-1-abelian-p-case}, for each $\beta_i$ (where $i \leq p-1$), there is a corresponding matrix $A_i \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{Z})$. We need to find a matrix $B \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{Z})$ such that $\overline{B}$ and all $\overline{A_i} + \overline{B}$ are invertible in $\mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$, for $i=1, \ldots, p-1$. Equivalently it is enough to show  that 
 \[
\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \neq \bigcup_{i=1}^{p-1} \big[(T -\overline{A_i}) \cap \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)\big], 
 \]
 where $T = \{X \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \mid \det X = 0\}$. For $i=1, \dots, p-1$,  let 
 \[
K_i= (T-\overline{A_i} ) \cap \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p),
 \]
 and $K_0= (T+ I_n) \cap \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$. (We could have $K_0$ being one of the $K_i$ for some $i$.) 
 So to prove the proposition it suffices to show 
\begin{equation}\label{eq.sum-invertible-eigenvalue1}
    \big|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)\big| > \big|\bigcup_{i=1}^{p-1} K_i\big|.
\end{equation}

We observe that $|K_i|= |K_0|$ for every $i$, as  the map $S \to -S (\overline{A_i})^{-1}$ provides  a bijection between $K_i$ and $K_0$. 

Let us note that 
\begin{align*}
K_0 &= \{ X+I_n=S \in GL_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \mid X \text{ singular } \} \\
&= \{ S \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \mid \det{(S-I_n)}=0 \}\\
&= \{ S \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \mid S v= v \, \, \text{ for some } \, 0 \neq v \in \mathbf{F}_{p}^n \}, 
\end{align*}
i.e. $K_0$ consists of those invertible matrices $S \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$ whose $1$ is an eigenvalue.

To compute the cardinality of $K_0$ we look at the set 
\[
R= \{ (S, v) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p) \times \mathbf{F}_p^{n, *} \mid  Sv = v \}, 
\]
where $ \mathbf{F}_p^{n, *} $ are the non-zero vectors of $\mathbf{F}_p^n$.
Note that $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$ acts transitively on $\mathbf{F}_p^{n, *}$ hence the Orbit-Stabilizer theorem implies that for any fixed $v \in \mathbf{F}_p^{n,*}$, the stabilizer $\mathrm{Stab}_v$  in $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)$ has order equal to  $\frac{|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|}{ |\mathbf{F}_p^{n,*}|}$,  as the orbit of $v$ is $\mathbf{F}_p^{n, *}$. 
Hence 
\[
|\mathrm{Stab}_v|= \frac{|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|}{p^n-1}
\]
and thus 
\begin{equation}\label{eq.|R|}
 |R| = \sum_{v \in \mathbf{F}_p^{n, *}}|\mathrm{Stab}_v|=  (p^n-1)|\mathrm{Stab}_v|=|\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|.    
\end{equation}


On the other hand, for any fixed $S \in K_0$ if $E_S$ is the eigenspace of $S$ for the eigenvalue $1$ then $|R|= \sum_{S \in K_0} (|E_S|-1)$. 
But for any $S \in K_0$ its eigenspace for $1$ has dimension at least $1$ and thus $|E_S| \geq p$. One of those matrices of $K_0$   is $I_n$ with $E_{I_n}=\mathbf{F}_p^n$. Hence 
\[
|R|= \sum_{S \in K_0} (|E_S|-1) \geq (|K_0|-1)(p-1)+ p^n-1.
\]
This, along with \eqref{eq.|R|} implies 
\[
|K_0|\leq  \frac{|GL_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|}{p-1} - \frac{p^n-1}{p-1} +1 <  \frac{|GL_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|}{p-1}, 
\]
where the last inequality is strict as $n \geq 2$.
So 
\[
\big| \bigcup_{i=1}^{p-1} K_i\big| \leq \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} |K_i| = (p-1) |K_0| < {|GL_n(\mathbf{F}_p)|}.
\]
This completes the proof of the proposition.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $1 \leq k < p-1$, it follows that $p \geq 3$, so $G$ has odd order and is therefore solvable. Now we proceed by induction on $|G|$. 

Let $N$ be a non-trivial minimal characteristic subgroup of $G$. Because $G$ is solvable $N$ must be  an elementary abelian $q$-group for some prime number $q$. To see this first observe that $N'$ is a characteristic proper (as $N$ is solvable) subgroup of $N$ and thus of $G$. Hence $N'=1$ forcing $N$ being abelian. As the Sylow subgroups of $N$ are characteristic we conclude that $N$ is an abelian $q$-group.  Similarly, the subgroup $\Omega_1(N) = \{ n \in N \mid n^q=1\}$ is characteristic in $N$ and so minimality forces $\Omega_1(N)= N$. Thus  
\[
N \cong \mathbf{Z}_q^n, 
\]
with $q \geq p$, since  $p$ is the smallest prime divisor of $|G|$. Consequently,  $k < p-1\leq q-1$. 

If $N=G$, then $G$ is an elementary abelian $q$-group, and the result follows directly from \autoref{Thm:k<p-1-abelian-p-case}. Hence we may assume that $N<G$.
Consider the quotient group $G/N$, whose smallest prime divisor is at least $p$. 
By induction $\mathcal{P}_k$ holds for $G/N$ and it also holds for $N$. Thus \autoref{prop: Extension-property} implies that $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$ completing the induction and the proof of the theorem.

label: lem:Sum-In-Zpn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Sum-In-Zpn}
Assume $p$ is a prime number and $n \geq 1$. Then 
\[    \sum_{x=1}^{p^n}  x^{p-1} \equiv -p^{n-1} \pmod{p^n}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first note that for $p=2$ the sum $\sum_{x \in \mathbf{Z}_{2^n}} x$ equals the unique nonzero involution  of $\mathbf{Z}_{2^n} $, that is the element $2^{n-1} \in \mathbf{Z}_{2^n}$ and so the lemma holds for $p=2$.

We may assume now that $p$ is odd and    we proceed by induction on $n$. The base case, $n=1$, is trivial:
\[
\sum_{x =1}^{p} x^{p-1} \equiv \sum_{x=1}^{p-1} 1 = p-1 \equiv -p^0 \pmod{p}.
\]
Assume the hypothesis holds for values less than $n$. We will now prove the inductive step for $n$. To compute the sum, we first split the elements of $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$ into two sets,  the set of units of the multiplicative  $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$ and the multiples of $p$:
\[
    \sum_{x=1}^{p^n} x^{p-1}= \sum_{(x,p)=1 \atop  1\leq x \leq p^n } x^{p-1} + \sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} (kp)^{p-1}.
\]

Applying the inductive hypothesis (for $n-1$)
                                                                              
the second part of the sum simplifies to:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} (kp)^{p-1}= p^{p-1} \sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} k^{p-1} = p^{p-1} ( rp^{n-1} -p^{n-2}),
\]
for some integer $r$. 
Since $p-1 \geq 2$, we have 
$\sum_{k=1}^{p^{n-1}} (kp)^{p-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{n}}$ and thus 
\[
\sum_{x=1}^{p^n} x^{p-1} \equiv  \sum_{(x,p)=1 \atop  1\leq x \leq p^n } x^{p-1} \pmod{p^n}.
\]

Now consider the endomorphism $\phi: \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^* \to \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$ defined by $\phi(x) = x^{p-1}$. Its kernel is 
\[\mathrm{Ker}(\phi)= \{ x \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^* \mid x^{p-1}= 1\}.
\]
Since $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$ is cyclic (as $p$ is odd), the order of the kernel is $p-1$. Given that $|\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*|= (p-1)p^{n-1}$, we know the size of  its  image  $|\mathrm{Im} (\phi)|=p^{n-1}$. Thus, each element in $\mathrm{Im} (\phi)$ has $p-1$ preimages in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$.

Consider the set $A \subseteq \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$ defined as 
\[
A=\{ 1+ sp \mid 0 \leq s< p^{n-1} \},  
\]
whose cardinality  is $p^{n-1}$.  Notice that every element $x \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}^*$ satisfies $x^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. Hence $\mathrm{Im} (\phi) \subseteq A$ and by cardinality $\mathrm{Im} (\phi) = A$. Hence 
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{(x,p)=1 \atop  1\leq x \leq p^n } x^{p-1} &=  (p-1) \sum _{s=0}^{p^{n-1}-1} (1+sp) \\
    &= (p-1) [p^{n-1} + p\sum_{s=0}^{p^{n-1}-1} s] \\
    &=  (p-1) [ p^{n-1} + p \frac{(p^{n-1}-1)p^{n-1}}{2}] \\
 &\equiv -p^{n-1} \pmod{p^n}.    
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.
head: environment

label: lem:PolynomialZero
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:PolynomialZero}
Let $p$ be a prime and $T(x) \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}[x]$ be a polynomial of degree at most $p-1$. If $T(x_i) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^n}$ for $p$ integers $x_1, \dots, x_p$ that are all nonequivalent modulo $p$, then $T(x)$ must be the zero polynomial.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $T(x)= a_0+a_1x+\dots +a_{p-1}x^{p-1}$ with $a_i \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$. The conditions $T(x_i)\equiv 0 \pmod{p^n}$ give the linear  system 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^{p-1}\\
1 & x_2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_2^{p-1}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
1 & x_p & x_p^2 & \cdots & x_p^{p-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
a_0\\
a_1\\
\vdots\\
a_{p-1}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\qquad\text{in } \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}.
\]
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is the Vandermonde determinant
\[
\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq p}(x_j-x_i).
\tag{5}
\]
Since the elements $x_1,\dots,x_p $ are pairwise distinct modulo $p$,
none of the differences $x_j-x_i$ is divisible by $p$. Hence every
$x_j-x_i$ is a unit in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$, and therefore the determinant  is also a unit in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$.
Thus the Vandermonde matrix  above is invertible over $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$. It follows
that $a_0=a_1=\cdots=a_{p-1}=0 $ in  $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$.
Therefore $T$ is the zero polynomial in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}[x]$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Cyclic-not-P_{p-1}}
Let $p$ be a prime and $n $ a positive integer. Then the  cyclic $p$-group $G=\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$ does not satisfy $\mathcal{P}_{p-1}$, and thus does not satisfy $\mathcal{P}_k$ for any $k \geq p-1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p=2$ the statement  is supported by the Hall-Paige theorem. For odd primes $p$, consider the automorphisms $\beta_i \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ defined by 
\[\beta_i(a)= ia,
\]
for $a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$ and $i=1, \dots , p-1$.
We assert that no bijection $f: G \to G$ exists such that the maps $a \mapsto ia+f(a)$ are bijections for all $i=1, \dots,p-1$.
Assume, for contradiction, that such a bijection $f: G \to G$ exists, meaning $a \mapsto ia+f(a)$ is a bijection for every $i=0,1,\dots,p-1$.

We define 
\[
T(x)= \sum_{a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}} \big(xa + f(a)\big)^{p-1}  - \sum_{a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}} a^{p-1}.
\]
Then $T(x) $ is a polynomial in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}[x]$ of degree $p-1$. 

Given that $ia+f(a)$ covers  all elements of $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$, for $a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$,  it follows that $T(i) = 0 \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$,  for all $i=1, \cdots,p-1$. Also $T(0) = 0$ because $f$ is a bijection of $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$. Applying   \autoref{lem:PolynomialZero} we conclude that  $T(x)$ must be the zero polynomial in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}[x]$.
But, expanding the binomials in the definition of $T(x)$, we see that the coefficient of $x^{p-1}$ equals  
\[
\sum_{a=1}^{p^n} a^{p-1} \equiv -p^{n-1} \pmod{p^n}. 
\]
As $ -p^{n-1} \not \equiv 0 \pmod{p^n}$ we reach a contradiction and thus proving the proposition.
head: environment

label: prop: Abelian-P_k
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: Abelian-P_k}
Assume $G$ is a finite abelian group satisfying $\mathcal{P}_k$.  Then for every prime $p$  with $p \leq k+1$ the Sylow $p$-subgroup $G_p$ is either  trivial or non-cyclic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume, for contradiction, that the abelian group $G$ does not satisfy the proposition. Thus, $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_k$ for some integer $k$, and its Sylow $p$-subgroup $G_p$ is cyclic for a prime $p \leq k+1$. This implies $k \geq p-1$, so $G$ satisfies $\mathcal{P}_{p-1}$. Let $G = G_p \times H$, where $H$ is an abelian group of order $m$ with $\gcd(m,p)=1$, and $G_p \cong \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$ with $n \geq 1$. Consider the automorphisms $B_i \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ defined by
\[
B_i (a,h)= (ia, h),  \,  \text{  for all } \, a \in G_p, \,  h \in H,  
\]
for $i=1, \cdots , p-1$.
 By assumption, there exists a bijection $F: G \to G$ such that $B_i + F$ is also a bijection of $G$ for all $i$. We write
 \[
 \pi: G \to \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}
 \]
 for the projection  of $G$  onto $G_p$ composed with the isomorphism $G_p \cong \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$ (we write $a$ for an element of $G_p$ and its isomorphic element in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}$). (So $\pi(B_i(a,h)) = ia$.)
 
 The fact that 
  $B_i + F$ is a bijection  for every $i$, implies that the multiset $\{\pi(B_i(g)+F(g))\mid g \in G\}$  picks every element of $Z_{p^n}$ exactly $m$-times and the same holds for the multiset $\{ \pi(F(g) ) \mid g \in G\}$.

  Similarly with the proof of \autoref{thm:Cyclic-not-P_{p-1}} we define 
 \[
T(x)= \sum_{g \in G } \big( x \pi(g)+ \pi (F(g)) \big)^{p-1}  - m\sum_{a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}} a^{p-1}.
\]
Then $T(x) $ is a polynomial in $\mathbf{Z}_{p^n}[x]$ of degree at most $p-1$. 
Furthermore 
\begin{align}
m \cdot \sum_{a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}} a^{p-1}&= \sum_{g \in G } \big( \pi( B_i(g) +F(g)) \big)^{p-1}=\sum_{g \in G } \big( \pi( B_i(g))  +\pi(F(g)) \big)^{p-1}\\
&= \sum_{h \in H } \sum_{a \in G_p} \big( i a + \pi (F((a,h)) \big)^{p-1}=\sum_{g \in G } \big( i \pi(g)+ \pi (F(g)) \big)^{p-1} .
\end{align}
 Hence $T(i)= 0$ for $i=1, \cdots p-1$. A similar argument shows that $T(0)=0$ because $F$ is a bijection of $G$. The rest of the proof follows th elinbes of that in \autoref{thm:Cyclic-not-P_{p-1}};  $T$ must be the zero polynomial by \autoref{lem:PolynomialZero}, while its leading coefficient is 
 \[
\sum_{g \in G} (\pi(g)) ^{p-1} = m \sum_{a \in \mathbf{Z}_{p^n}}  a^{p-1} \equiv -mp^{n-1} \pmod {p^n}.
 \]
As $(m,p)=1$ the leading coefficient is not zero contradicting the conclusion $T=0$. The proposition now follows.

\label{quest:1}
 Let $G$ be a finite abelian $p$-group. Is it true that $G$ satisfies
$\mathcal{P}_{p-1}$ if and only if $G$ is noncyclic? Equivalently, does every
noncyclic finite abelian $p$-group satisfy $\mathcal{P}_{p-1}$?

label: Thm:CommonTrans
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:CommonTrans}
Assume $G$ is a finite abelian group so that $G= X\oplus Y$ with $|X|=|Y|=m$. Assume further that $\{Z_j\}_{j \leq k}$   are subgroups of $G$ of the same order $m$ that intersect trivially both $X$ and $Y$. If $k \leq p-2$, where $p$ is the smallest prime divisor of  $m$, then the  collection of subgroups $\{ X, Y, Z_j \mid j \leq k \}$ share a transversal in $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by noting that $G = X \oplus Z_j = Y \oplus Z_j$ for all $j=1, \dots, k$. Hence $X \cong Y$. 
We fix an enumeration $X = \{ x_1, \cdots, x_m\}$ of $X$  and we enumerate the elements of $Y$ with respect of the fixed enumeration of $X$ and the isomorphism $X \cong Y$ (that is,  if $x_i +x_j=x_t$ then $y_i +y_j=y_t$).  
Now we claim that for every $j=1, \dots,  k$,  the elements of the subgroup $Z_j$ can be written as 
\[
Z_j= \{ z_i^j= x_i+ \theta_j(y_i)  \mid i \leq m \}
\]
for some automorphism $\theta_j \in \mathrm{Aut}(Y)$. 



To prove the claim, we fix $j$ and we  first observe that every element $z \in Z_j$  has a unique expression $z=x+y$ with $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$  and  distinct elements $z_1, z_2 \in Z_j$ do not share the same $X$ or $Y$-part (as $Z_j \cap X = Z_j \cap Y = \{0\}$).  Hence we can enumerate the elements of $Z_j$ with respect to their $X$-part as 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:z=x+y}
z_i^j =x_i + \theta_j(y_i),
\end{equation}
where $\theta_j$ is a bijection of $Y$. To complete the proof of the claim it remains to show that $\theta_j$ are actually homomorphisms.  But if $z_t^j=z_i^j +z_{i'}^j $,  for some $t$,  then $x_i+x_{i'}=x_t$ and  $ \theta_j(y_i) +\theta_j(y_{i'})= \theta_j(y_t)=\theta_j(y_i+y_{i'}) $, with the last equality following from the way we enumerated $Y$. This proves the claim.

According to \autoref{Thm:main}, there exists a bijection $f:Y \to Y$ so that $f-\theta_j$ are also bijections of $Y$ for all $j=1, \dots, k$, as $k \leq p-2$. Take the set 
\[
F=\{ x_i +f(y_i) \mid i \leq m \}. 
\]
we will show that $F$ is a common transversal for all subgroups  $X, Y, Z_j $, with $1 \leq j \leq k$.  
Clearly $F$ is a transversal of  $X$ (as $f$ is a bijection) and of $Y$. For a fixed $j$, using \eqref{eq:z=x+y} we get  
\[
x_i+f(y_i) \equiv -\theta_j(y_i) +f(y_i) \pmod {Z_j}.
 \]
Because $f-\theta_j$ are bijections for all $j$, all the elements of $F$ are nonequivalent modulo $Z_j$ and thus $F$ is a transversal of $Z_j$.
This completes the proof of the theorem.
